assignments.title: 28.1 Critical Questions: Livy, History of Rome
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read each excerpt below and answer the question that follows it. Write three to five sentences for each answer, in your own words. Use evidence from the excerpt and from your lessons. If you are unsure about part of your answer, say so and explain what you would need to know. That is good thinking, not a mistake.

Excerpt 1

The beginning of freedom should be dated from the fact that the power of the consuls was made yearly, and not from any lessening of the power the kings had held. The first consuls kept all the rights and signs of rule that the kings had had.

Livy, History of Rome, book 2, chapter 1 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 1. Livy says freedom began because the consuls' power lasted only a year, not because it was made smaller. Using the lesson “From Romulus to the Republic”, explain why a limit on time might protect Romans from a king as well as a limit on power would have, and what dangers might still remain.

Excerpt 2

Once, when the parts of the human body did not all agree as they do now, the other parts grew angry that all their care and labor went to feed the belly, while the belly sat idle in the middle and enjoyed what they brought. They agreed that the hands should carry no food to the mouth, nor the mouth take it, nor the teeth chew it. But while they tried to starve the belly into obeying, the limbs and the whole body wasted away. Then they saw that the belly's work was not idle. It was fed, and it fed them in turn, sending back to every part the blood by which we live.

Livy, History of Rome, book 2, chapter 32 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 2. Livy says this story was told to plebeians who had marched out of Rome. In your own words, explain what the speaker wants them to think about patricians and plebeians. Then use the lesson “From Romulus to the Republic” to give one reason the plebeians might not have been fully satisfied by the story alone.

Your verdict

Question 3. Livy says Rome became free by limiting the time a ruler could hold power. Is a limit on time enough to keep a people free? Take a side, and defend it using Livy and the lesson “From Romulus to the Republic”. Say what the strongest argument against your view would be.

assignments.title: 28.2 Primary Source Exercise: Polybius, The Roman Constitution
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

If we look at the power of the consuls, the government seems entirely kingly. If we look at the Senate, it seems an aristocracy. And if we look at the power of the people, it seems plainly a democracy.

Each of these three parts can either hinder or help the others. None of them can act alone, and none can work against the rest without being checked. So the government is well fitted to meet every emergency, and it is hard to find a better one.

Polybius, Histories, book 6, chapters 11 and 18 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Polybius was a Greek who lived in Rome as a young man.

Question 1. Explain in your own words how Polybius says the three parts of the Roman government depend on one another. Then use the lesson “Consuls, Senate, and People” to give one example of a check that one part had on another, and say whether it matches his description.

Question 2. Polybius was a Greek who had been taken to Rome and who admired what he saw. Name one way this might make him a good observer and one way it might lead him to miss or to overlook something. Use the lesson “Consuls, Senate, and People”, for example what it says about who counted as a citizen, to support your answer.

assignments.title: 29.1 Critical Questions: Livy, History of Rome
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read each excerpt below and answer the question that follows it. Write three to five sentences for each answer, in your own words. Use evidence from the excerpt and from your lessons. If you are unsure about part of your answer, say so and explain what you would need to know. That is good thinking, not a mistake.

Excerpt 1

He was found plowing his land. After greetings were exchanged, the messengers said, "May the gods bless you and your country. The Senate asks that you put on your toga and hear its orders." Astonished, he asked, "Is all well?" and told his wife to bring his toga from the hut. He wiped the dust and sweat from himself, put it on, and came forward. Then the messengers hailed him as dictator.

Livy, History of Rome, book 3, chapter 26 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 1. Livy takes care to show Cincinnatus at work on his own land when the Senate calls him. Using the lesson “The Legion and the Conquest of Italy”, explain why Livy and the Romans who loved this story might have wanted readers to picture him this way.

Excerpt 2

The dictator, who had been named for six months, laid down his office on the sixteenth day, having ended the war and saved the army.

Livy, History of Rome, book 3, chapter 29 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 2. Suppose Cincinnatus had kept his office for the full six months, or longer. Using this excerpt and the lessons “Consuls, Senate, and People” and “The Legion and the Conquest of Italy”, explain what the Romans trusted a dictator to do, and what a Roman might have feared if he had not given up power.

Your verdict

Question 3. Was Cincinnatus' giving up power admirable, or only what any good Roman citizen was expected to do? Take a side, and defend it using Livy and the lessons “Consuls, Senate, and People” and “The Legion and the Conquest of Italy”. Say what the strongest argument against your view would be.

assignments.title: 29.2 Primary Source Exercise: Polybius, The Romans Build a Navy
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

It was at this time that the Romans first thought seriously of the sea. They had no ships and no skill at rowing, yet they dared to try. They began with such boldness that before they had ever tried the sea they challenged the Carthaginians, who had held command of it for generations.

A ship of the Carthaginians had run aground, and the Romans used it as a model. They built a hundred large ships, and while the ships were being built they seated the crews on rowing benches on dry land and taught them to row by drill.

Polybius, Histories, book 1, chapters 20 and 21 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Polybius was a Greek who wrote about the rise of Rome.

Question 1. Polybius says the Romans challenged Carthage at sea before they had ever tried the sea. Use this passage and the lesson “Rome and Carthage: The First Punic War” to explain what this shows about Roman boldness, and what weakness the corvus was meant to make up for.

Question 2. Polybius was a Greek who admired Rome, yet the lesson “Rome and Carthage: The First Punic War” says he thought it was unjust for Rome to seize Sardinia and Corsica. Explain how that fact affects how far you would trust his praise of Roman boldness here, and what a writer who both admires and criticizes a people can tell us.

assignments.title: 30.1 Critical Questions: Polybius, Histories
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read each excerpt below and answer the question that follows it. Write three to five sentences for each answer, in your own words. Use evidence from the excerpt and from your lessons. If you are unsure about part of your answer, say so and explain what you would need to know. That is good thinking, not a mistake.

Excerpt 1

Hannibal saw that his soldiers were downcast from the long march and its hardships. He called them together and, having no other encouragement to give, showed them Italy, which lies so close beneath the Alps that, seen together, the mountains seem to be the walls of the whole country. He pointed out the plains of the Po, and reminded them of the friendly feeling of the Gauls who lived there, and he pointed the way to Rome itself. By this he lifted their spirits.

Polybius, Histories, book 3, chapter 54 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 1. From the top of the Alps, Hannibal points to Italy and to Rome. Using the lesson “Hannibal Crosses the Alps”, explain what he wants his tired soldiers to feel, and why that mattered so much for an army so far from home.

Excerpt 2

When Hannibal set out from Spain he had about ninety thousand foot soldiers and twelve thousand horsemen. But when he came down into Italy he had in all only about twenty thousand foot soldiers and not more than six thousand horsemen.

Polybius, Histories, book 3, chapters 35 and 56 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Polybius says he took the figures from a record Hannibal himself set up.

Question 2. Compare the two sets of numbers. Using the lesson “Hannibal Crosses the Alps”, explain what they show about the cost of the march, and why a general who arrives with so many fewer men might have to win by trick and not by size.

Your verdict

Question 3. Was Hannibal a great man? Take a side, say what you mean by greatness, and defend your view using Polybius and the lesson “Hannibal Crosses the Alps”. Say what the strongest argument against your view would be.

assignments.title: 30.2 Primary Source Exercise: Polybius, The Battle of Zama
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

Hannibal said to Scipio: "Consider how quickly fortune can change. I myself stand before you as an example. I once fought you in Italy and had your whole country in fear, and now I am here to ask for the lives of my people. You are young and have never been beaten. But a wise man does not trust his good luck at the height of his success."

In that battle Hannibal acted as a skilled and tried general should. He had used every resource before the fight, and he held nothing back. But he was beaten.

Polybius, Histories, book 15, around chapters 6 and 16 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Polybius was a friend of Scipio's family.

Question 1. Hannibal warns Scipio how quickly fortune can change. Explain what he is asking Scipio to do and why he thinks it is wise. Then use the lesson “Fabius, Scipio, and Zama” to tell what Scipio actually did, and whether the later lives of the two men show that Hannibal's warning applied to Scipio too.

Question 2. Use the passage and the lessons “Hannibal Crosses the Alps” and “Fabius, Scipio, and Zama” to give your own answer to this week's question: was Hannibal a genius, a gambler, or both? Give one piece of evidence on each side. Then say what you would want to check, since a friend of Scipio's family is giving us this judgment.

assignments.title: 31.1 Critical Questions: Plutarch, Life of Tiberius Gracchus
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read each excerpt below and answer the question that follows it. Write three to five sentences for each answer, in your own words. Use evidence from the excerpt and from your lessons. If you are unsure about part of your answer, say so and explain what you would need to know. That is good thinking, not a mistake.

Excerpt 1

The wild beasts that roam over Italy have each a den to lie in, but the men who fight and die for Italy have nothing but air and light. Without house or home they wander about with their wives and children. They fight and die to give wealth and comfort to others. They are called the masters of the world, and they have not a clod of earth that is their own.

Plutarch, Life of Tiberius Gracchus, chapter 9 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Plutarch was a Greek who wrote about Rome long after these events.

Question 1. Plutarch gives Tiberius these words about Roman soldiers. Using the lesson “Carthage Destroyed, Greece Conquered”, explain who the soldiers were and what had happened to their farms, and why a speech like this might make rich senators afraid.

Excerpt 2

The rich, by offering higher prices, took the land of the poor, or seized it by force, and they worked great estates with bought slaves in place of free farmers. The free men of Italy, who were also its soldiers, grew fewer, and the country was filled with slaves.

Plutarch, Life of Tiberius Gracchus, chapter 8 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Plutarch was a Greek who wrote about Rome long after these events.

Question 2. Suppose slaves had been scarce and costly after the wars. Using this excerpt and the lesson “Carthage Destroyed, Greece Conquered”, explain how that might have changed what happened to Roman farmers, and why the Gracchi might still have found a problem to fix.

Your verdict

Question 3. Were the Gracchi right to take land from the rich to help the poor? Take a side, and defend it using Plutarch and the lesson “Carthage Destroyed, Greece Conquered”. Say what the strongest argument against your view would be.

assignments.title: 31.2 Primary Source Exercise: Sallust, The Jugurthine War
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

Jugurtha left the city. It is said that as he went he often looked back at it in silence, and at last he said, "A city for sale, and soon to perish if it finds a buyer."

Before the destruction of Carthage, the Roman people and the Senate managed the state peacefully among themselves, and there was no struggle for glory or power. Fear of the enemy kept the citizens in good conduct. But when that fear had left their minds, the things that good fortune loves, license and pride, began to grow.

Sallust, The Jugurthine War, chapters 35 and 41 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Sallust was a Roman who wrote many decades after the war.

Question 1. Sallust says fear of Carthage kept Romans honest and that after Carthage fell, license and pride grew. Explain his argument, then use the lessons “Carthage Destroyed, Greece Conquered” and “Marius and the Army of the Poor” to give one example from each lesson that fits it, and one point where you think the argument is too simple.

Question 2. Sallust says Jugurtha is said to have called Rome a city for sale, yet Sallust could not have heard it himself, and he wrote sharply about greed among the nobles. Explain how far you would trust the quotation, and what the story could still tell us even if the words are not exact. Use what you learned in the lesson “Marius and the Army of the Poor” to support your answer.

assignments.title: 32.1 Critical Questions: Plutarch, Life of Crassus
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read each excerpt below and answer the question that follows it. Write three to five sentences for each answer, in your own words. Use evidence from the excerpt and from your lessons. If you are unsure about part of your answer, say so and explain what you would need to know. That is good thinking, not a mistake.

Excerpt 1

Crassus bought houses that were burning, and the houses near them, since their owners would sell cheaply in fear. In this way he came to own a great part of Rome. He used to say that no man is rich who cannot support an army from his own income.

Plutarch, Life of Crassus, chapter 2 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Plutarch was a Greek who wrote about Rome long after these events.

Question 1. Crassus says no one is rich who cannot support an army from his own income. Using the lesson “Spartacus, Pompey, and the First Triumvirate”, explain what this shows about how money and armies were connected in the late Republic, and why that might worry the Senate.

Excerpt 2

Pompey, who came upon some of the runaways as they fled, wrote to the Senate that Crassus had beaten the slaves in open battle, but that he himself had pulled the war up by the roots.

Plutarch, Life of Crassus, chapter 11 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Plutarch was a Greek who wrote about Rome long after these events.

Question 2. Suppose Pompey had not written that letter. Using the excerpt and the lesson “Spartacus, Pompey, and the First Triumvirate”, explain what the letter shows about what the generals wanted from a victory, and how it might have changed the way Romans saw Pompey.

Your verdict

Question 3. Is great wealth a danger to a republic? Take a side, and defend it using Plutarch and the lesson “Spartacus, Pompey, and the First Triumvirate”. Say what the strongest argument against your view would be.

assignments.title: 32.2 Primary Source Exercise: Caesar, The Gallic War
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

Caesar saw that the hill could not be taken by assault, so he ordered works to be built all around it. He had a ditch dug twenty feet wide with straight sides, and behind it a rampart with a wall and towers. When he learned that a great Gallic army was coming to relieve the hill, he ordered a second line of the same kind, facing outward, so that even a vast force could not surround his men.

Vercingetorix called a council and said that he had made the war not for his own needs but for the common freedom, and that since fortune must be yielded to, he offered himself to the Romans, to be put to death or handed over as they pleased. Caesar sat on the rampart in front of the camp, and the leaders were brought out, and Vercingetorix was handed over.

Caesar, The Gallic War, book 7, chapters 72 to 74 and 89 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Caesar wrote this account himself, and he calls himself Caesar.

Question 1. Explain what this passage shows about Caesar's skill, and about how he wants Romans to see him. Notice that he writes "Caesar" and not "I." Using the lesson “Caesar in Gaul”, say what effect that might have on his Roman readers.

Question 2. Caesar reports a speech by his enemy Vercingetorix about the common freedom. Explain how far you would trust Caesar's report of it. Then name something about the cost of the war that the lesson “Caesar in Gaul” says this passage leaves out, and say what that tells us about reading a general's own account.

Use evidence from the excerpt and from your lessons. If you are unsure about part of your answer, say so and explain what you would need to know. That is good thinking, not a mistake.

Excerpt 1

When he came to the river Rubicon, which divides Gaul from Italy, he stopped. He began to think how great a step he was taking, and he stood in silence, weighing the choice, and spoke with the friends beside him. Then he said, "We can still turn back, but once we cross this little bridge, everything must be settled by the sword."

Plutarch, Life of Caesar, chapter 32 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Plutarch was a Greek who wrote about Caesar long after these events.

Question 1. Plutarch says Caesar stopped at the river and talked over the choice with his friends. Using the lesson “Crossing the Rubicon”, explain what Caesar might have faced if he had turned back, and what this tells you about how much choice he really had.

Excerpt 2

Caesar called the soldiers together. He reminded them of the wrongs his enemies had done him, and said that the tribunes of the people, who had stood up for him, had been driven from the city by force. He asked them to defend the good name and honor of the general under whom, for nine years, they had served the state with great success.

Caesar, The Civil War, book 1, chapter 7 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Caesar wrote this account himself, and he calls himself Caesar.

Question 2. Caesar tells his soldiers that he is defending his honor and the rights of the tribunes. Using the lesson “Crossing the Rubicon”, explain why Caesar would want his readers to see the war this way, and how the Senate might say the same events should be understood.

Your verdict

Question 3. Was Caesar's crossing of the Rubicon a defense of his honor or an attack on his country? Take a side, and defend it using the excerpts and the lesson “Crossing the Rubicon”. Say what the strongest argument against your view would be.

assignments.title: 33.2 Primary Source Exercise: Plutarch and Suetonius on Caesar
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

Antony, who was one of the runners, made his way through the crowd and held out a crown wound with laurel. A few people clapped, and it was plain that they had been told to. When Caesar pushed it away, all the people applauded. Antony offered it again, and again only a few clapped, but when Caesar refused it, all applauded again. The trial, it seemed, had failed, and Caesar rose and ordered the crown carried to the Capitol.

He even let slip the saying that the Republic was nothing, a mere name without body or form.

Plutarch, Life of Caesar, chapter 61, and Suetonius, Life of the Deified Julius, chapter 77 (both adapted from public-domain translations). Both writers lived more than a century after Caesar's death.

Question 1. Plutarch says only a few people clapped when the crown was offered, and everyone clapped when Caesar refused it. Using the lesson “Dictator for Life and the Ides of March”, explain what this scene might tell us about how the crowd felt about kings, and name one thing about it that we cannot know.

Question 2. Suetonius says Caesar let slip that the Republic was a mere name. Explain how far you would trust this report, since Suetonius wrote long afterward and lived under emperors. Then use the lesson “Dictator for Life and the Ides of March” to explain how such a saying would fit the reasons Brutus and Cassius gave for the killing, even if Caesar never said it.

assignments.title: 34.1 Critical Questions: Appian and Plutarch
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read each excerpt below and answer the question that follows it. Write three to five sentences for each answer, in your own words. Use evidence from the excerpt and from your lessons. If you are unsure about part of your answer, say so and explain what you would need to know. That is good thinking, not a mistake.

Excerpt 1

Whoever kills one of the proscribed and brings the head shall receive, if he is a free man, twenty-five thousand Attic drachmas. If he is a slave, he shall receive his freedom, ten thousand drachmas, and the citizen name of his master. The same rewards shall go to informers. Those who hide or help any of the proscribed shall themselves be put on the list.

Appian, Civil Wars, book 4, chapter 11 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Appian was a Greek who wrote about the Roman civil wars long after they ended.

Question 1. The edict offers money to free killers, freedom to slaves, and a threat to anyone who hides the proscribed. Using the lesson “Octavian, Antony, and the Second Triumvirate”, explain what the Triumvirs hoped these rewards and threats would do to ordinary Romans, and what dangers came with them.

Excerpt 2

Antony ordered that Cicero's head and hands be cut off, the hands that had written the speeches against him. When they were brought, he looked on them with joy and laughed, and he ordered them fastened up above the speakers' platform in the Forum. The Romans shuddered at the sight, for they thought they saw not the face of Cicero, but an image of Antony's soul.

Plutarch, Life of Cicero, chapters 48 and 49 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Plutarch was a Greek who wrote about Cicero about a hundred and fifty years after his death.

Question 2. Plutarch says the Romans shuddered when they saw Cicero's head and hands in the Forum. Using the lesson “Octavian, Antony, and the Second Triumvirate”, explain why Antony wanted them put there, and what this display tells us about how the Republic had changed.

Your verdict

Question 3. Is any cause great enough to justify the proscriptions? Take a side, and defend it using the edict, Plutarch, and the lesson “Octavian, Antony, and the Second Triumvirate”. Say what the strongest argument against your view would be.

assignments.title: 34.2 Primary Source Exercise: Augustus, Res Gestae
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

At the age of nineteen, on my own decision and at my own cost, I raised an army, and with it I set free the Republic, which had been oppressed by the tyranny of a faction.

In my sixth and seventh consulships, when I had put an end to the civil wars, I handed the state over from my own power to the control of the Senate and the Roman people. For this service I was named Augustus by decree of the Senate. After that time I stood above all in influence, but I had no more power than the others who were my colleagues in each office.

Augustus, Res Gestae (Deeds of the Divine Augustus), chapters 1 and 34 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Augustus wrote this near the end of his life.

Question 1. Augustus says he handed the state back and had no more power than his colleagues. Using the lesson “Actium and the First Emperor”, explain what he gave up in 27 BC and what he kept, and say whether "no more power than the others" is a fair description.

Question 2. Augustus says that at nineteen he freed the Republic from "the tyranny of a faction." Using the lessons “Octavian, Antony, and the Second Triumvirate” and “Actium and the First Emperor”, name one thing about how he rose that this sentence leaves out. Then explain how far this makes you trust the text, and what it is still good evidence for.

assignments.title: 35.1 Critical Questions: Virgil and Juvenal
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read each excerpt below and answer the question that follows it. Write three to five sentences for each answer, in your own words. Use evidence from the excerpt and from your lessons. If you are unsure about part of your answer, say so and explain what you would need to know. That is good thinking, not a mistake.

Excerpt 1

Others, I believe, will shape bronze to breathe more softly and carve living faces from marble. They will plead in court better, and trace the paths of the sky and tell the rising stars. You, Roman, remember to rule the peoples with your power. These will be your arts: to set the custom of peace, to spare the conquered, and to beat down the proud.

Virgil, Aeneid, book 6, lines 847 to 853 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Virgil was a Roman poet who wrote in the time of Augustus.

Question 1. Virgil says that Rome's arts are to set the custom of peace, to spare the conquered, and to beat down the proud. Using the lesson “The Pax Romana: Governing an Empire”, give one example of how Rome set the custom of peace in its provinces. Then say what a person living in a province might add to Virgil's list.

Excerpt 2

The people who once gave out commands, high office, legions, everything, now hold back and eagerly wish for only two things: bread and circus games.

Juvenal, Satire 10, lines 77 to 81 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Juvenal was a Roman poet who mocked the faults of his city, about a century after Augustus.

Question 2. Juvenal complains that the people who once gave out commands and offices now care only for bread and games. Using the lessons “Consuls, Senate, and People” and “The Pax Romana: Governing an Empire”, explain what the Roman people had once done in the Republic, why rulers were glad to give them bread and games, and what this shows about the change from Republic to empire.

Your verdict

Question 3. Was Roman rule a gift to the world, or a theft from it? Take a side, and defend it using Virgil, Juvenal, and the lesson “The Pax Romana: Governing an Empire”. Say what the strongest argument against your view would be.

assignments.title: 35.2 Primary Source Exercise: Tacitus, Agricola
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

Calgacus said: "Robbers of the world, they have taken everything, and now that the land has nothing left for them they search the sea. If an enemy is rich, they are greedy. If he is poor, they want glory. East and West have not satisfied them. To plunder, to butcher, to steal, they falsely call empire, and where they make a desert, they call it peace."

Little by little the Britons were led to the things that make people soft: the colonnades, the baths, and the elegant dinner party. The simple natives called this "civilization," when it was part of their slavery.

Tacitus, Agricola, chapters 30 and 21 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Tacitus was a Roman historian and the son-in-law of Agricola, the Roman general in Britain.

Question 1. Tacitus was the son-in-law of the Roman general in Britain, yet he wrote this speech for a British chief. Using the lesson “Rome’s Frontiers: Germans, Jews, and Persians”, explain how far you would trust that these are Calgacus's real words, and what Tacitus might have wanted his Roman readers to think about.

Question 2. The lesson “The Pax Romana: Governing an Empire” says Rome governed with a light touch and that baths were public places to relax. Using Tacitus's second paragraph and the lessons “The Pax Romana: Governing an Empire” and “Rome’s Frontiers: Germans, Jews, and Persians”, explain how the same baths and towns might look different to a Roman and to a Briton, and name one thing we still could not know.

assignments.title: 36.1 Critical Questions: Pliny and Trajan
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read each excerpt below and answer the question that follows it. Write three to five sentences for each answer, in your own words. Use evidence from the excerpt and from your lessons. If you are unsure about part of your answer, say so and explain what you would need to know. That is good thinking, not a mistake.

Excerpt 1

They said that the whole of their guilt or error was this: they were accustomed to meet on a fixed day before dawn and sing a hymn to Christ as to a god, and to bind themselves by an oath, not to do any wicked deed, but not to commit theft, robbery, or adultery, not to break their word, and not to refuse to return a deposit when asked.

Pliny the Younger, Letters, book 10, letter 96 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Pliny was a Roman governor writing to the emperor Trajan from a province in what is now Turkey, about AD 112.

Question 1. Pliny reports what the Christians told him about their meetings, and he found nothing worse. Using the lesson “Christianity in the Roman World”, explain what Pliny still asked them to do, and why that was a test of loyalty and not of crime.

Excerpt 2

You have followed the right course in your examination of these cases. No fixed rule can be laid down. They are not to be hunted out. If they are brought before you and the charge is proved, they must be punished. But if anyone denies that he is a Christian and proves it by worshiping our gods, he is to be pardoned, however suspect his past.

Trajan to Pliny, Letters, book 10, letter 97 (adapted from a public-domain translation). This is the emperor's reply.

Question 2. Suppose Trajan had ordered governors to hunt down Christians in every town. Using his actual reply and the lesson “Christianity in the Roman World”, explain how things might have been different for Christians, and why Trajan may have chosen not to give that order.

Your verdict

Question 3. Was Trajan's reply to Pliny just? Take a side, and say what a fairer rule would have looked like, using the excerpts and the lesson “Christianity in the Roman World”. Say what the strongest argument against your view would be.

assignments.title: 36.2 Primary Source Exercise: Lactantius and Eusebius
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

Constantine was warned in a dream to mark the heavenly sign of God on the shields of his soldiers, and so to go into battle. He did as he was told. With a slanting letter X, its top bent round, he marked the name of Christ on their shields. Armed with this sign, his army took up their swords.

He said that about the middle of the day, when the sun was beginning to turn, he saw with his own eyes the sign of a cross of light in the sky, above the sun, and with it the words, "By this, conquer." He said that he and the whole army with him were amazed. He doubted at first what the sign could mean. Then, in the night, Christ appeared to him with the same sign, and told him to make a copy of it and use it as a protection against his enemies.

Lactantius, On the Deaths of the Persecutors, chapter 44, and Eusebius, Life of Constantine, book 1, chapters 28 and 29 (both adapted from public-domain translations). Both writers were Christians who wrote soon after the events, and Eusebius says Constantine told him the story himself, long afterward.

Question 1. Compare the two accounts. Name one thing they agree on and one thing they tell differently. Then use the lesson “Constantine and the Christian Empire” to explain why a historian cannot simply choose the account that sounds best.

Question 2. Eusebius says Constantine told him the story himself, long afterward. Explain how that might make the story more believable and how it might make it less believable. Then use the lesson “Constantine and the Christian Empire” to say what Constantine's later actions add to the question of whether he truly believed.

quizzes.title: 28.1 Reading Quiz: From Romulus to the Republic

questions.text: The Romans told stories about Aeneas and about Romulus and Remus, and Livy wrote them down about seven hundred years after the events. What should a careful reader conclude about these stories?

answers.text: They are exact history, because Livy was a Roman and knew his own city.
They show what the Romans believed about themselves, even if we cannot be sure they are exact history.
They are false, so they teach us nothing at all.
They were written down at the time of Romulus.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says we cannot be sure how much is true. Diggers found huts from about that time, so a village really existed, but Livy used old stories passed from person to person. The tales still show that the Romans saw themselves as tough, loyal, and proud.

questions.text: After the king fled in 509 BC, the Romans did not choose a new king. They chose two consuls who each served for one year. What does this choice suggest?

answers.text: They wanted a faster way to fight their wars.
They had no one in the city who could lead.
They hoped the Etruscans would soon return.
They feared one man holding power for long, so they split power and limited the time.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Rome could have kept a king, as other Italian cities did. Choosing two officials with short terms shows that the Romans no longer trusted any one man with lasting power.

questions.text: In 494 BC the plebeians marched out of the city and refused to fight or work. Why did the patricians have to listen?

answers.text: Rome needed the plebeians' labor and their spears.
The plebeians had taken over the Senate.
The Etruscans had joined the plebeians against Rome.
The patricians had already agreed to give up their offices.

questions.feedback_general: The plebeians were the great majority. They were farmers, craftsmen, and shopkeepers, and they fought in the army. Without them Rome could not work or fight, so the two sides agreed that the plebeians could choose tribunes.

questions.text: Historians who admire the Roman Republic often point to the Conflict of the Orders as a source of Roman strength. What about it do they admire?

answers.text: It ended quickly after one great battle.
The plebeians won every right they wanted at once.
Both sides bargained and gave something up, so it never became a civil war.
The patricians kept all the power, and the plebeians stopped asking.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the struggle lasted about two hundred years and that patricians gave way a little at a time. Because both sides bargained, Rome avoided civil war. This habit of compromise is what admirers praise.

questions.text: The Twelve Tables were sometimes harsh. Why did the lesson still call their greatest value so important?

answers.text: They made sure only patrician judges knew the law.
Everyone could now read the laws, which made it harder for a powerful person to twist them.
They ended debt and slavery in Rome.
They gave plebeians the right to be consul at once.

questions.feedback_general: The plebeians had complained that the laws were secret and that patrician judges could bend them. Once the laws were written and displayed in the Forum, they bound everyone. The lesson calls this idea the rule of law.

quizzes.title: 28.2 Reading Quiz: Consuls, Senate, and People

questions.text: Each consul could stop the other, and a consul had to step down after a year. What problem were the Romans trying to solve?

answers.text: Too few men were willing to take office.
The high cost of paying officials.
The danger of one man holding power like a king.
The need to make decisions more quickly in war.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the Romans feared that one man with too much power would act like a king. So they set short terms, split the work among many hands, and let each consul check the other.

questions.text: The Senate could not pass laws by itself, but its advice carried great weight. What helps explain this?

answers.text: Senators served for life and so knew more about government than any one-year consul.
Senators commanded the army.
Senators were chosen by lot every year.
Senators could remove the tribunes.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says most senators were former officials, and they served for life. A consul stayed in office only a year, so he leaned on the Senate's experience.

questions.text: A dictator held full power, but only for six months. Why did the Romans trust such an office?

answers.text: The consuls watched over every decision a dictator made.
Dictators were always young men with little power of their own.
The Senate named a dictator only in times of peace.
They believed good men would give up power when the danger passed.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the Romans trusted this office because they believed good men would give up power once the emergency was over. It sets up next week's story of a man who did exactly that.

questions.text: Polybius thought Rome's government blended kingly, aristocratic, and democratic parts. Why did he think this mixture made Rome stable?

answers.text: It let the strongest part rule without any check.
Each part could check the others and needed the others to get anything done.
It copied the government of Athens exactly.
It gave all the power to the common people.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says each part could check the others and each needed the others. Polybius believed this mixture gave Rome more stability than any one kind of government alone.

questions.text: A Roman farmer could vote, serve as a soldier, and perhaps one day be elected. Even so, the lesson says the share of people who truly ruled was smaller than the whole population. Why?

answers.text: Only patricians were allowed to vote.
Farmers were not allowed to take part in the assemblies.
Rome had no assemblies at all.
Women, children, slaves, and many foreigners could not vote or hold office.

questions.feedback_general: Only free adult men who were citizens could both vote and hold office. Born citizens who were women had some legal rights but no vote. Slaves had no rights. As in Athens, the ruling group was smaller than the population.

quizzes.title: 29.1 Reading Quiz: The Legion and the Conquest of Italy

questions.text: Roman soldiers were citizens who owned land and bought their own weapons. Why did that make them fight so hard?

answers.text: A lost battle might cost a farmer his own home, so he had every reason to win.
They were paid higher wages than any hired soldier in the world.
The law forced them to fight all year long.
They hoped that each victory would make them dictator.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says that because they fought for their own farms, they fought hard. A farmer who lost a battle might lose his home.

questions.text: About 390 BC the Gauls burned much of Rome. What did the Romans do afterward, and what does it show?

answers.text: They gave up the city and moved away.
They made peace and stopped training.
They rebuilt, put up strong walls, and trained harder.
They asked the Etruscans to rule them.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the disaster could have been the end of the city, but the Romans rebuilt, put up strong walls, and trained harder. It shows a stubbornness that Rome would need again.

questions.text: A legion was split into maniples that stood in rows with gaps, like the squares on a checkerboard. Why did this help on rough ground?

answers.text: Soldiers in a legion carried much longer spears.
Each maniple could move on its own, and the next line could step forward if one was pushed back.
A legion was so small that it could hide.
A legion only fought on flat, open plains.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says a maniple could move on its own, so a legion could handle rough ground better than a tight phalanx. If one line was pushed back, the next stepped forward.

questions.text: After a victory, Rome often made the losers allies and asked for soldiers instead of tribute. Why was this a smart choice?

answers.text: It made the allies rich enough to rebel.
It gave Rome gold to spend on a navy.
It let Rome avoid all further wars.
Each victory made Rome's army larger, and the allies had something to lose if Rome fell.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says each victory made Rome's army larger. Allies kept their lands, laws, and pride, so even defeated enemies had a reason to stay loyal.

questions.text: Pyrrhus beat the Romans in two battles, yet he went home in 275 BC. What explains this?

answers.text: The Romans had more elephants than he did.
His elephants refused to fight a third time.
Rome could raise more troops from its allies, but he could not replace his lost men.
The Greek cities of the south joined Rome before the first battle.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says each win cost him many of his best men. Rome kept raising troops from its allies, and he could not. That is why a win that costs too much is called a Pyrrhic victory.

quizzes.title: 29.2 Reading Quiz: Rome and Carthage, the First Punic War

questions.text: Most of Carthage's troops were mercenaries. Why might that be a weakness compared with Rome's army?

answers.text: Mercenaries were never given weapons.
They were always badly trained.
Carthaginians would not let them fight at sea.
They fought well when paid, but had less reason to die for the city.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says they fought well when paid but had less reason to die for Carthage. Roman citizen-soldiers were fighting for their own homes.

questions.text: Rome had a big land army but almost no ships, and many observers would have bet on Carthage. Yet Rome voted to help at Messana. What does this suggest about the Romans?

answers.text: The Senate was united and sure of an easy win.
They were willing to risk a war they were not ready for, and they hated to give up.
Carthage had promised to give Rome the island.
Rome already had the largest navy in the Mediterranean.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the Senate argued, because the war would be against Carthage, and that the Romans were stubborn and did not like to give up.

questions.text: The raven, or corvus, let Roman soldiers fight on an enemy deck as if on land. Why was this a good fit for Rome?

answers.text: Roman crews lacked skill at handling ships but were strong at close fighting on solid ground.
The raven made Roman ships faster than Carthaginian ships.
The raven let Roman ships stay far away from the enemy.
The raven made it unnecessary to build a navy.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the Romans lacked skill at ships, so they fitted a boarding bridge with a spike and used what they knew best. At Mylae in 260 BC this trick won the first Roman naval victory.

questions.text: Rome lost more ships to storms than to Carthage, and its treasury ran dry. What made a last fleet possible?

answers.text: A loan from Carthage.
A new tax on Sicily.
Rich Romans lent their own money, to be repaid only if Rome won.
Silver brought from Spain.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says rich citizens lent money of their own to build another fleet, with a reward only if Rome won. That fleet crushed the Carthaginians at the Aegates Islands in 241 BC.

questions.text: Polybius himself thought one Roman act after the war was unjust. Which act was it?

answers.text: Seizing Sardinia and Corsica while Carthage was too weak to resist.
Making Sicily a Roman province.
Asking Carthage to pay a large sum over many years.
Sending Regulus to Africa.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Rome took Sardinia and Corsica while Carthage was fighting its own mercenaries, though Rome had no good reason. Hamilcar Barca came home angry, and his young son Hannibal was watching.

  • Explain the plan of Fabius and why many Romans hated it.

quizzes.title: 30.1 Reading Quiz: Hannibal Crosses the Alps

questions.text: Hannibal ate what his soldiers ate and slept on the ground in his cloak. What does this suggest about why his army followed him?

answers.text: He was a rich man who paid them better than anyone.
Their laws forced them to obey any general.
He shared their hardships, so they loved and trusted him.
He kept them from learning how dangerous the march would be.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the soldiers loved him and that he ate what they ate and slept on the ground. A leader who shares hardship earns loyalty that money cannot buy.

questions.text: Rome ruled the sea, so Hannibal could not sail an army to Italy. What did that force him to do?

answers.text: March his army by land through Gaul and across the Alps.
Wait in Spain until the Romans attacked.
Ask Carthage to send a second fleet.
Make peace with Rome before the war began.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says he decided to march, over the Pyrenees, through Gaul, across the Rhone, and over the Alps in late autumn.

questions.text: Polybius says Hannibal reached Italy with only about twenty thousand foot soldiers and six thousand horsemen, out of a much larger army. What can we infer?

answers.text: The Romans had destroyed part of his army earlier.
Hannibal sent most of his men home on purpose.
The march was very costly, so he could not hope to win by numbers alone.
The Alps were easy to cross.

questions.feedback_general: Some men were left to guard Spain, but many were lost on the march. The lesson says Hannibal knew he could not match Rome in numbers and had to use his wits.

questions.text: At Cannae the Romans put their strongest troops in the center and planned to push straight through. How did Hannibal use that plan against them?

answers.text: He ran away and left the field.
He put his best men in the center to block them.
He used elephants to break the Roman center.
He let his weaker center bend back while his strong sides and cavalry closed around the Romans.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the Romans were drawn into a pocket and then surrounded, packed so tightly that their numbers meant nothing. This is called a double envelopment.

questions.text: After Cannae, Maharbal said Hannibal knew how to win a victory but not how to use one. What reasons does the lesson give for doubting that Hannibal could simply have taken Rome?

answers.text: Rome had already made peace.
He had no siege machines, Rome had strong walls, and his small army was far from home.
His elephants were too weak to move.
Carthage had sent a second army to take his place.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson lists these reasons, and adds that Hannibal needed help from Carthage that never came. It says historians still argue about it and that we cannot know the answer.

quizzes.title: 30.2 Reading Quiz: Fabius, Scipio, and Zama

questions.text: Fabius followed Hannibal at a safe distance and avoided a big fight, and many Romans hated this plan. Why did they later see he had been right?

answers.text: He beat Hannibal quickly in the end.
Hannibal could win any open fight, so Rome needed to deny him one.
His term as dictator had ended.
Hannibal ran out of elephants.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says that after Cannae the Romans saw that Hannibal could win any open fight. Delay bought Rome the time it needed.

questions.text: Hannibal hoped that Rome's allies would leave it after his big wins, but most stayed loyal. What helps explain this?

answers.text: Hannibal's army treated their lands very gently.
They feared Roman punishment more than anything else.
Rome paid them large sums each year.
They had long been partners of Rome, keeping their own governments and sharing in its spoils.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says that for two hundred years Rome had treated its allies as partners. Hannibal was a foreign general with a small army far from home. This is the payoff of the system studied in the week before.

questions.text: Scipio was about twenty-five when the people sent him to Spain, though he held no high office. What does this tell us about Rome in that crisis?

answers.text: Romans were willing to bend their usual rules to put a gifted man in command.
Rome always chose its youngest men as generals.
Rome had no other commanders left alive.
The Senate chose him because he was a priest.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson calls it an unusual choice. His father and uncle had been killed in Spain, and the crisis made Romans willing to set the usual path aside.

questions.text: Hannibal would not leave Italy, so Scipio landed his army in North Africa. Why was this a good answer?

answers.text: It forced Carthage to call Hannibal home to defend the city.
It let Scipio capture Hannibal's army in Italy.
It stopped Carthage from trading with Spain.
It gave Rome a chance to rest its soldiers.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Carthage panicked and called Hannibal home, and the two armies met at Zama in 202 BC. Some senators, including Fabius, thought the plan too risky.

questions.text: Both Hannibal and Scipio ended their lives in bitterness or exile. What does the lesson suggest about the Republic?

answers.text: The Senate always rewarded success.
Carthage's government was stronger than Rome's.
Exile is the usual end for good generals.
A man who won too much glory could become a threat, and the old habit of sharing power needed leaders who stayed among equals.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson ends with this warning. Rivals envied Scipio and accused him of taking bribes. It says the Republic would struggle with this problem over the next century.

quizzes.title: 31.1 Reading Quiz: Carthage Destroyed, Greece Conquered

questions.text: Many historians doubt that Carthage was a danger in 149 BC, yet Rome destroyed it. What does the lesson suggest explains Rome's act?

answers.text: Fear and pride, since Romans had not forgotten Hannibal.
Carthage had attacked Rome first.
Carthage had built a new war fleet.
Carthage had refused to pay anything for fifty years.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Carthage had given up its empire, its navy, and its army, and it was no threat. Fear and pride pushed Rome to a cruel act, and some Romans felt uneasy about it.

questions.text: After 146 BC, many Romans admired Greek learning and copied Greek buildings. How had the Greeks' own situation changed?

answers.text: They taught Roman governors how to rule.
They became equal citizens of Rome.
They kept their full independence.
They answered to a Roman governor, and the freedom of the city-states was finished.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Greece was now part of the Roman world. Admiration did not give Greek cities their freedom back.

questions.text: Wars now lasted for years across the sea. Why did that ruin many Roman farmers?

answers.text: Farmers were forbidden to own land.
A farmer away at war for years saw his farm fail, and many had to sell their land.
Slaves took the farmers' places in the army.
The Senate taxed farms out of existence.

questions.feedback_general: The citizen-soldier used to serve for a season and go home. Now he might be away a long time, and Hannibal's army had also burned fields in Italy.

questions.text: Rich Romans bought up land and built great estates worked by slaves. Why could a free farmer not compete?

answers.text: Slaves were taught better farming than free men.
Free farmers refused to sell their grain.
Slaves were cheap and could work all year, while a farmer had only his own two hands.
The Senate banned free farmers from the markets.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says slaves were captured in the wars and cost little. Many families lost their farms and drifted to Rome, where there was little work.

questions.text: Tiberius Gracchus had a rival tribune removed from office, which broke a custom. What was the effect?

answers.text: It made the Senate love him.
It ended the quarrel between rich and poor.
It made the veto stronger.
It made his enemies fear him more, and violence soon entered Roman politics.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says that breaking the custom made his enemies fear him more, and that he was later clubbed to death. It was the first time in generations that Romans had killed each other over politics.

quizzes.title: 31.2 Reading Quiz: Marius and the Army of the Poor

questions.text: Jugurtha bribed senators, and Sallust says he called Rome a city for sale. Why did ordinary Romans grow furious?

answers.text: Jugurtha refused to pay tribute to Rome.
Senators refused to go to Numidia.
Their sons were dying in wars while nobles were taking bribes.
Marius himself had taken a bribe.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the war dragged on while generals made deals with Jugurtha or failed to win. People began to ask for someone who would not take bribes.

questions.text: Marius was a new man from the small town of Arpinum who said openly that the nobles were weak. Why did the voters turn to him?

answers.text: He was a rich nobleman.
He did not come from the old noble families and had won fame as a soldier.
He was the choice of the Senate.
He had already ended the war in Numidia.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says he came from outside the noble families and had a soldier's fame. In 107 BC the voters made him consul, and he brought the war to an end.

questions.text: Marius let poor men without property join the army. Why was this both smart and dangerous?

answers.text: It lowered the pay of every soldier.
It made the Senate stronger.
It forced the Senate to give every soldier land.
It gave Rome plenty of soldiers, but landless soldiers looked to their general for pay and a future.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says a soldier with no land had nothing to go back to, and the Senate often refused him land. The only person who could help him was his general.

questions.text: Marius was elected consul five years in a row, though custom said a man should wait ten years. What does the lesson draw from this?

answers.text: Rome could survive danger only by breaking its own rules, and each emergency gave one man more power.
Marius had cheated in every election.
The Senate had given up its power on purpose.
Roman custom had no force at all.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says that danger had become a habit. Each emergency gave one man more power.

questions.text: In 88 BC Sulla led his army to the gates of Rome and entered the city. What did this show?

answers.text: That Roman soldiers never obeyed a general.
That a general with loyal legions could seize the city, and the laws could not stop him.
That the Social War was over.
That the Senate had asked him to defend the city.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says no Roman general had ever done this before. Sulla later became dictator with no six-month limit, and he showed that the laws could not stop a general with loyal legions.

quizzes.title: 32.1 Reading Quiz: Spartacus, Pompey, and the First Triumvirate

questions.text: Spartacus began with about seventy runaways, and his army grew to tens of thousands. What can we infer about slavery in Italy?

answers.text: Few slaves wished to be free.
Slaves were treated kindly on the estates.
Slaves were never allowed to fight.
There were many slaves, often captured in Rome's wars, ready to join anyone who broke free.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Italy held hundreds of thousands of slaves by the 70s BC and that slaves from farms and estates flocked to the rebels.

questions.text: The sources disagree about what Spartacus wanted. What should a careful reader do?

answers.text: Say that we cannot be certain, and weigh the accounts instead of choosing the one that sounds best.
Choose the account that makes him a hero.
Ignore the revolt, since no one knows what he wanted.
Trust whatever Crassus said about him.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson gives two accounts. In one he hoped to lead his people out of Italy over the Alps. In the other the runaways wished to stay and plunder. It says we do not know for certain.

questions.text: After the revolt, about six thousand captured slaves were nailed to crosses along the road from Capua to Rome. What was the purpose?

answers.text: To honor the dead.
To mark the road for travelers.
To serve as a warning, though cruelty made the fear greater.
To pay the soldiers of Crassus.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the crosses were meant as a warning. It adds that cruelty made the fear greater and that no one in the Senate could see a way to end it.

questions.text: Pompey was made consul in 70 BC though he was too young and had not held the lower offices. What does this show?

answers.text: Romans had never cared about age.
Romans were willing to bend the rules for a successful general, and such a man might not return to being an ordinary citizen.
The Senate no longer met.
Pompey had been a tribune for many years.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the Senate began to fear him. The old rule was that a general gave up his command when a war ended, and Pompey, like Sulla, made many Romans wonder whether that rule still held.

questions.text: The First Triumvirate was a private pact among Caesar, Pompey, and Crassus. Why did it matter?

answers.text: Real decisions were now made in private by three men, and the Senate was bypassed.
It was an official office that replaced the consuls.
It ended the quarrels between the three men.
It gave the plebeians a new tribune.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the Republic's offices still existed, but the real decisions were made by three men in a secret deal. Each needed the other two, and none could be sure the pact would last.

quizzes.title: 32.2 Reading Quiz: Caesar in Gaul

questions.text: After his year as consul, Caesar had huge debts and needed a province. Why was Gaul a good choice for him?

answers.text: The Senate forced him to go there.
A war there could win him glory, wealth to pay his debts, and an army loyal to him.
Gaul was already at peace and easy to govern.
Pompey ordered him to go.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says a governor had an army, a chance for glory, and a way to get rich. Caesar saw how Sulla and Pompey rose, and he meant to do the same.

questions.text: Caesar built a bridge across the Rhine in ten days and landed in Britain, though these brought little. Why did he bother?

answers.text: To conquer Germany.
To find gold.
Because Rome loved a daring story, and each bold deed made him more famous at home.
Because the Senate demanded it.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Caesar knew that Rome loved a daring story, and that such deeds made him famous where his rivals could not match him.

questions.text: Caesar wrote the Commentaries in the third person and called himself Caesar. How should a careful reader take them?

answers.text: As a source with a point of view, since he was a politician who needed support at home.
As a neutral report with no point of view.
As proof that everything he said was false.
As a book written by someone else.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the third person makes the book sound as if a neutral reporter were describing the facts. But Caesar made himself look wise, brave, and just. This does not mean he lied all the time, only that we should ask what he wanted Romans to believe.

questions.text: At Alesia, Caesar built one wall facing inward and a second wall facing outward. Why?

answers.text: To keep his own soldiers from deserting.
To keep out the Parthians.
To hold prisoners for his victory parade.
To keep Vercingetorix's army inside and to guard against the Gallic army coming to rescue it.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Caesar was trapped between two armies, and that after days of hard fighting the Romans held.

questions.text: Julia died and Crassus was killed at Carrhae. What happened to the triumvirate?

answers.text: Caesar and Pompey became closer friends.
Pompey moved to Gaul.
Two of the ties that held it together were gone, and Pompey and Caesar began to look at each other with suspicion.
The Senate made it an official office.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says only Pompey and Caesar remained. Pompey stayed near Rome with the Senate leaning toward him, and Caesar was far away with an army.

quizzes.title: 33.1 Reading Quiz: Crossing the Rubicon

questions.text: Caesar asked to run for consul while still in Gaul with his army, and the Senate said no. Why did that refusal worry him so much?

answers.text: He would have to pay a large fine to the Senate.
Pompey would take over his province at once.
Once his command ended he would be a private man, and his enemies could take him to court and ruin or exile him.
He would be forbidden to enter Italy for ten years.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Caesar needed to come home and run for consul again, but as soon as his command ended his enemies could take him to court for what he had done as consul. A man in court could be ruined, even exiled.

questions.text: The lesson says each side thought the other was the aggressor, and that neither would give way. What does this suggest about the coming of the war?

answers.text: Both sides could have stepped back, and neither did, so each helped bring the war on.
Only the Senate wanted a war.
Caesar had planned the war for years and no one could stop him.
Nothing anyone did could have prevented it.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the Senate could have let Caesar run for consul and the war might have been avoided, and that Caesar could have turned back. It says the Republic died because Roman leaders had spent years refusing to trust one another.

questions.text: Caesar says he was defending his honor and the tribunes' rights, while Plutarch makes the crossing a dramatic gamble. Why might their stories differ?

answers.text: Plutarch was at the river and Caesar was not.
Caesar never wrote about the war.
Both wrote at the same time for the same readers.
Each writer shaped the story to what he wanted readers to feel.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says each version is shaped by what the writer wanted readers to feel. Caesar wrote about his own war, and Plutarch wrote about 150 years later.

questions.text: At Pharsalus Pompey had far more men, yet he lost. What does the lesson give as part of the reason?

answers.text: Pompey had no horsemen at all.
Caesar's veterans had fought together for years and held steady, and a hidden line of his best foot soldiers turned back the horsemen.
Caesar had a much larger fleet.
The Senate refused to send Pompey supplies.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Pompey's horsemen charged and were turned back by a hidden line, and then his army broke and ran. Steady, experienced soldiers mattered more than numbers on paper.

questions.text: Caesar pardoned many of his captured enemies, but Cato refused any pardon and later took his own life. What might Cato's choice show?

answers.text: Cato wanted to become Caesar's friend.
Pardons were never offered in Roman wars.
He thought that accepting mercy from Caesar meant accepting that Caesar had the right to rule over him, and he would not.
He was afraid of dying in battle.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Cato was the strictest senator and kept fighting rather than accept a pardon, and that he took his own life rather than live under Caesar. For him, mercy from one man was a sign that the Republic's rules no longer held.

quizzes.title: 33.2 Reading Quiz: Dictator for Life and the Ides of March

questions.text: The Senate gave Caesar statues, a golden chair, and a purple robe, and then named him dictator for life. Why did these honors alarm old Romans?

answers.text: They cost the Senate too much money.
The honors were meant for gods and not for men.
Caesar had refused all honors until then.
Each new honor made Caesar look less like a fellow citizen and more like a ruler.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says each new honor made Caesar look less like a fellow citizen and more like a ruler. Rome's old dictators served only six months, but a dictator for life had no limit.

questions.text: At the Wolf Festival Antony offered Caesar a crown, and Caesar pushed it away twice. What is the best reading of this scene?

answers.text: It proves that Caesar wanted to be king.
We cannot be sure what it meant, but Romans who remembered the old kings would have been uneasy either way.
It proves that it was only a joke.
It shows that Antony wanted to be king himself.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says ancient writers could not agree whether it was a test of the crowd or a show planned in advance. It adds that to many senators a ruler who could not be removed was a king in all but name.

questions.text: Brutus had been forgiven by Caesar, yet he joined the plot. What reason does the lesson give?

answers.text: He believed that if one man could grant or take away life at will, Romans were no longer free citizens.
He wanted to become dictator himself.
He thought that mercy was a sign of weakness.
He felt he owed Caesar nothing and was angry about it.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Brutus believed a Roman's first duty was to the city and its laws, not to any person. He thought that being spared by Caesar proved the problem.

questions.text: What did the assassins fail to do?

answers.text: They failed to choose a day when the Senate was meeting.
They failed to ask Caesar's soldiers to join them beforehand.
They thought only about the killing and made no plan for Antony, the army, or the city.
They failed to name Brutus dictator at once.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the assassins thought only about the knife and almost nothing about the morning after. They had no army and no plan to win over Caesar's soldiers, and they hoped the Republic would simply return.

questions.text: Why did the crowd turn against the assassins after Caesar's death?

answers.text: Brutus's speech was too long.
The Senate declared that Caesar was a god.
Cassius spoke against Caesar's will.
Antony read out Caesar's will, which left money to every citizen, and showed the crowd the bloody robe.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Antony, a gifted speaker, read out the will and showed the robe. The crowd grew furious and burned the body in the Forum, and Brutus and Cassius had to flee.

quizzes.title: 34.1 Reading Quiz: Octavian, Antony, and the Second Triumvirate

questions.text: Octavian was young, often sick, and no great soldier, yet within months he had an army. What explains this?

answers.text: The Senate gave him command of its legions.
Caesar's veterans heard the name of their old general and rallied to his son.
He paid his soldiers out of his own treasure.
Antony lent him a legion as a gift.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Caesar's name was worth more than gold, and soldiers who had served under Caesar would follow his son almost anywhere.

questions.text: Cicero hoped to use Octavian against Antony and then push him aside. Why did that plan fail?

answers.text: Octavian refused to meet with anyone.
Cicero was killed before he could speak again.
Antony beat Octavian in the first battle.
Octavian made peace with Antony, because each man had something the others needed.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says that in 43 BC Octavian made peace with Antony. Antony had experience and an army, Lepidus had troops near Rome, and Octavian had the name of Caesar.

questions.text: The lesson says the Second Triumvirate was different from the first. What was the difference?

answers.text: It was made legal by a vote, so each man held great power and no one could check him.
It was a private deal with no real power.
It included Cicero as a fourth member.
It was meant to last for the lifetime of its members.

questions.feedback_general: The first triumvirate, with Pompey, Caesar, and Crassus, was a private deal. This one was made legal by a vote, and it was to last five years.

questions.text: Why did the three men publish the lists called proscriptions?

answers.text: To make a record of Romans who had died in the wars.
To give the Senate more power over the army.
To pay their armies from the dead men's property and to take revenge on their enemies.
To protect Rome from enemies outside Italy.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says they wanted money for their armies and revenge on their enemies. The killer was paid, and the state took the dead man's property to buy loyalty.

questions.text: Appian tells of slaves who betrayed their masters, and also of wives and slaves who risked their lives to save people on the lists. What can we infer?

answers.text: All Romans behaved cruelly during the proscriptions.
The terror pushed some people to betray and others to risk everything for those they loved.
Nobody dared to help anyone on the lists.
Appian made up the loyal ones to improve his story.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson reports both kinds of stories. Fear and reward brought out the worst in some people and the best in others.

quizzes.title: 34.2 Reading Quiz: Actium and the First Emperor

questions.text: Octavian declared war on Cleopatra, not on Antony. Why was that clever?

answers.text: It let him avoid fighting at sea.
It made Antony his ally.
It made the war look like a fight against a foreign enemy and not another civil war.
It forced the Senate to give up its power.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says that this made it look like a war against a foreign enemy, and that it worked. After years of civil war, Romans were tired of Romans killing Romans.

questions.text: Octavian made Egypt his own property, and no senator could enter without his leave. What does this suggest?

answers.text: Egypt was too poor to matter.
Senators did not like to travel.
Egypt had no grain.
Egypt's grain fed Rome, so whoever held Egypt held the key to the city's food, and he did not want a rival to gain a base there.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the grain of the Nile would feed Rome, and that he would hold the key. Keeping senators out kept any rival from using Egypt against him.

questions.text: In 27 BC the Senate looked after the peaceful lands and Augustus held the provinces where most of the army was stationed. What does this show?

answers.text: Real power stayed with the man who held the army, whatever the old names said.
Real power had moved back to the Senate.
The people now held the real power.
Augustus had no army left.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson calls this the heart of the matter. The Republic's offices and names stayed, but the man with the legions held the power.

questions.text: Augustus wrote a long list of his deeds called the Res Gestae. Why should a careful reader not rely on it alone?

answers.text: It was written in a language that nobody could read.
A man who lists his own deeds chooses what to include, and this one leaves out the proscriptions.
It was written by his enemies.
It says nothing about temples or games.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says he is not lying about the temples or the games, but a list of one's own deeds is not a neutral report. We should ask what he leaves out and what he wants readers to think.

questions.text: The lesson says few people noticed the change from Republic to rule by one man, and that was what Augustus wanted. Why would he want that?

answers.text: Romans loved kings and wanted one.
The Senate had begged to be ruled.
He wanted to be remembered as harsh.
Romans hated the idea of a king, and Caesar had been killed for looking like one.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Augustus had seen what happened to Caesar. By keeping the old offices, names, and costumes, he held a king's power without a king's title.
